title: Natural selection acts on variation in populations
learning_objectives: Explain natural selection using heritable variation and differential reproductive success.
Distinguish population change across generations from an individual changing because it needs to.
Apply the mechanism to a new environmental pressure.

sources.title: Natural selection
sources.publisher: Understanding Evolution, University of California Museum of Paleontology

misconceptions.description: Individual organisms evolve the traits they need during their lifetimes.
Natural selection intentionally gives organisms useful traits.

critical_errors.description: Claims that need or effort directly creates a heritable adaptive trait in an individual.
Describes natural selection as a purposeful agent with a future goal.

teaching_brief.goal: Help the learner explain natural selection as a population-level generational process.
teaching_brief.learner_profile: A beginner who uses phrases such as 'the animal adapted because it needed to.'
instructions: Use an example with pre-existing heritable variation.
Track survival or reproduction across multiple generations.
Contrast individual acclimation with evolutionary change.
Ask the learner to explain a new case without purpose-driven language.
prohibited_disclosures: Do not reveal held-out item wording.
Do not imply that natural selection plans ahead.

pretest.prompt: In a beetle population, color is heritable and birds more often catch green beetles than brown beetles. What directly changes first?

choices.text: Every green beetle turns brown.
Brown beetles leave a larger share of offspring.
Birds intentionally create brown mutations.
The population stops reproducing.

pretest.prompt: Which statement describes evolution by natural selection?

choices.text: Individuals practice until a useful trait becomes genetic.
Heritable variants differ in reproductive success, changing variant frequencies.
A species chooses traits needed for the future.
All mutations appear because the environment requests them.

posttest.prompt: Why does antibiotic resistance become common in a bacterial population?

choices.text: Individual bacteria decide to resist the drug.
Antibiotics teach every bacterium the same mutation.
Resistant variants survive and reproduce more under treatment.
The population has a future goal of resistance.

posttest.prompt: Which condition is necessary for natural selection to change a trait distribution?

choices.text: Relevant variation must be heritable.
Every individual must change equally.
The environment must know the best future trait.
No reproduction may occur.

transfer.prompt: A drought leaves mostly hard seeds. Birds already vary in heritable beak strength. Which sequence is natural selection?

choices.text: All birds strengthen their beaks by trying, then transmit the exercise.
Stronger-beaked birds obtain more food and leave more offspring, so the trait becomes more common.
The drought designs stronger beaks.
Birds choose the population's future genes.

transfer.prompt: A person develops larger muscles through training. Why is this not by itself evolution by natural selection?

choices.text: It is an acquired change in one individual, not demonstrated heritable population change across generations.
Muscles never vary.
Natural selection happens only in bacteria.
Exercise prevents reproduction.
heritable variation through differences in reproductive success
future plans chosen by a species
traits acquired by effort in every individual
only harmful traits

retention.prompt: Where is an evolutionary change measured?

choices.text: In trait or allele frequencies in a population across generations
Only in one organism's intentions
In the environment's goals
In how hard one organism tries
